$meta.note: One entry per stimulus. `description` is shown above the sketch. `prediction` is the block-1 question, anchored on this scene's object and outcome, and is reused verbatim in block 3 after the imposed change so both blocks target the same outcome. `outcome` is the same outcome as a noun clause, slotted into the block-2 question. `imposed` is the block-3 counterfactual clause. All four are given to the model verbatim. ALL NEED AUTHOR REVIEW before launch, against study/stimuli-contact-sheet.html.
descriptionRules: Name the objects and how they are arranged. Never state or hint at what happens next.
Call the drawing convention 'the motion arrow', the same wording as the instructions screen.

Avoid the vocabulary of the concept list (friction, bouncy, stiff, pivot, balance point, heavier): describe objects in everyday words, so the description cannot supply the answer the list is meant to measure.
questionRules: prediction: name the object and the outcome, never the property being varied. 'What happens next?' alone is ambiguous in timescale (people segment an event at several nested grains), so two participants answer different questions; naming the target collapses that variance (Battaglia et al. 2013 ask 'Will it fall?' and 'In which direction?', not an open question).

outcome: the same outcome as a noun clause, so block 2 can fix the outcome while leaving the change free. This is what keeps the participant's chosen attribute as the measurement (RQ2) while making answers comparable across participants.
Never two questions in one stem: lay respondents answer such items inconsistently (Adams et al. 2006, CLASS).
